processing: A loose regional name rather than one defined method. The Izumo area is best known for matcha and everyday tea, and processing follows whichever type is being made.
harvest_season: As with most Japanese green tea, the spring picking is the prized one; little is documented about local picking dates.
appearance_dry: Varies with the type; leaf teas are typically dark green needles, matcha a fine green powder.
appearance_liquor: Typically yellow-green for leaf tea; matcha gives an opaque green bowl.
appearance_wet: Typical of Japanese green tea: soft green leaf fragments.
taste_profile: No single profile is documented. Expect the fresh, vegetal, gently savoury character usual for Japanese green tea, varying with the type.

brewing.notes: General guidance for a Japanese leaf green tea. Matcha from the area is whisked instead.

vintage_note: No fixed vintage practice is documented for this name. As with other Japanese green teas, leaf tea is usually sold from the current year's harvest and is best drunk fresh, with new-crop spring tea the most sought after.
description:
Izumo-cha means tea from the Izumo side of Shimane, on the Sea of Japan coast. It is a small name next to Shizuoka or Uji, and it is more a regional label than a defined style.

What makes the area interesting is less the leaf than the drinking culture. Matsue, the old castle town, is known for how much tea it drinks, and matcha there is treated as an everyday drink rather than a ceremony-only one.

Little is documented about a distinct taste, so go by the type on the label. A leaf tea should brew like other Japanese greens, with cooler water and a short first steep; matcha gets whisked.

When buying, ask what the tea actually is and where the leaf was grown, since the name alone tells you little. The local dish to try alongside is botebote-cha, a frothed tea eaten with small bits of food.
history:
The documented story is about tea drinking around Matsue. City history material says the Matsue domain treated tea as a luxury under its thrift orders and at times forbade townspeople and farmers to drink it, with stories of commoners drinking in secret.

The lord Matsudaira Harusato (Fumai) was a noted tea man, and his influence is the usual explanation for the strong tea habit in Matsue today, though the same city material warns against assuming so simple a link. Little is documented about the name Izumo-cha itself.
